These notes develop the mathematical foundations of **topological data
analysis (TDA)** through computational algebraic topology. Starting from
distance and continuity, we build towards cubical homology, persistence,
stability, and image-based applications. They are intended for readers with
some mathematical maturity, but no prior knowledge of topology.

**Work in progress.** Every planned chapter currently has a draft, but this
TDA section is still under development. The exposition, notation, proofs,
examples, exercises, and implementations may change as the notes are revised.

::: {.callout-important title="Bachelor's thesis and repository"}
The contents of these notes are based on my BSc Mathematics thesis,
*Computational Stability of Cubical Homology: Orthogonal Controls for Fault
Isolation in Retinal Diagnostics*. The public thesis and its accompanying code
and materials are available below.

[Read the bachelor's thesis](thesis/Nieto_TDA_Public_20260430.pdf){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank" rel="noopener"}
[Open the project repository](https://github.com/reyjosephnieto/ph){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank" rel="noopener"}

I have adapted and reorganised the thesis into this developing set of notes so
that I can expand the exposition gradually. A thesis has strict length
constraints, which limited how fully I could motivate definitions, develop
examples, and explain proofs. Here, I intend to fill those gaps and make the
material accessible to readers whose mathematical background consists of
basic calculus.

The presentation is organised as a course: definitions are introduced before
they are used, proofs are separated from implementation, and the retinal
application appears only after the necessary mathematical foundations.
:::

The central idea is to turn geometric and topological questions into finite
algebraic computations. In particular, we will study why

$$
\partial_k \circ \partial_{k+1}=0
$$

and how this identity leads to homology groups, algorithms, filtrations, and
persistent homology.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read these notes"}
The chapters are cumulative, but they are not meant to be read at a uniform
speed. A first encounter with metric spaces, quotient spaces, or functors can
feel much more abstract than the image-processing problem that motivated
them. When that happens, keep the following concrete dictionary in view:

| Abstract object | Picture to keep in mind |
|---|---|
| metric | a rule for deciding how different two points or images are |
| open neighbourhood | the points allowed by a chosen tolerance |
| complex | pixels together with their edges and vertices |
| chain | a selected collection of cells |
| boundary map | “keep only the perimeter” |
| homology class | a loop or component after filled-in boundaries are ignored |
| filtration | a thresholded image growing one level at a time |
| persistence interval | the lifespan of one topological feature |

On a first reading, concentrate on the examples and the statements of the
results. Proofs marked as sketches and the final chapter on category theory
can be revisited after the computational pipeline is familiar. None of the
applications requires the reader to become fluent in categorical notation
immediately.
:::

## The route through the subject

The course repeatedly moves through the same four levels:

$$
\text{distance and continuity}
\longrightarrow
\text{finite shapes}
\longrightarrow
\text{linear algebra}
\longrightarrow
\text{stable image descriptors}.
$$

Metric and topological spaces provide the language of closeness and
deformation. Graphs and cell complexes replace continuous shapes by finite
objects. Linear algebra turns their boundaries into matrices. Persistent
homology then follows the resulting features through an image filtration,
while stability theory tells us how sensitive those features are to changes
in the data.

## Why turn topology into vectors?

Neural networks and most other statistical learning methods ultimately operate
on numerical inputs. A digital image is already a numerical array, and the
usual neural-network architecture for image data is a convolutional neural
network (CNN). A CNN repeatedly transforms pixel arrays into learned numerical
features. We will not develop that machinery here.

Convolutional networks are effective at learning local visual patterns and can,
in principle, learn information related to shape and topology. Standard CNN
architectures, however, do not explicitly represent connected components,
loops, or voids, nor do they ordinarily guarantee that these quantities are
preserved through their learned transformations. When those structures matter,
it is useful to provide them to a learning system directly rather than require
the network to rediscover them from pixels.

The pipeline developed in these notes therefore has the form

$$
\text{digital image}
\longrightarrow
\text{cubical filtration}
\longrightarrow
\text{persistence diagrams}
\longrightarrow
\text{topological vector}
\longrightarrow
\text{statistical or neural model}.
$$

The topological vector is a fixed-length numerical summary of components,
loops, and their persistence across thresholds. It can be concatenated with
ordinary image or geometric features, used as an interpretable auxiliary
input, or studied independently with a simple classifier.

Producing numbers is not enough: the conversion must also be stable. If two
images differ only by a minute, physically insignificant perturbation, we
would like their topological vectors to remain close. In schematic form, the
desired guarantee is

$$
\text{small image change}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{small topological-vector change}.
$$

Establishing when this implication holds—and identifying when sampling,
interpolation, or an unstable vectorisation can break it—is one of the main
purposes of the metric, persistence, and stability chapters.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof-oriented presentation"}
These notes follow the convention of a typical undergraduate mathematics
course: definitions fix the objects under discussion; lemmas isolate useful
steps; propositions and theorems state the main conclusions; and proofs make
the logical dependence explicit. Results proved in the thesis source are
included here whenever they fit the level and scope of the chapter. A proof
sketch is labelled as such when a complete proof requires machinery developed
elsewhere.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Why the development is cubical"}
Many introductions to computational topology develop the subject primarily
through **simplicial complexes**. This is the standard and more flexible
language: simplices can model arbitrary meshes and combinatorial spaces
without requiring an underlying rectangular grid.

These notes instead develop the main constructions first for **cubical
complexes**. This is a deliberate choice motivated by the application.
Digital images are already made of pixels, and volumetric images are made of
voxels; these are naturally $2$- and $3$-dimensional cubes. A cubical model
therefore preserves the native geometry and adjacency structure of the data,
without first subdividing every pixel or voxel into simplices.

The two viewpoints are not competing theories. Cubical complexes can be
triangulated, and the later chapter on
[functoriality and triangulation](functoriality-triangulation/index.qmd)
explains how the Coxeter--Freudenthal--Kuhn construction passes from cubes to
simplices while preserving the relevant chain and homology structure. Thus
the cubical development remains connected to the broader simplicial theory,
while keeping the image-based motivation visible from the outset.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Sources and attribution"}
The exposition and chapter sequence are my own adaptation of the thesis, but
the mathematical development relies heavily on two principal sources:

- Vidit Nanda's *Computational Algebraic Topology* lecture notes
  [@nanda2023]; and
- Kaczynski, Mischaikow, and Mrozek's *Computational Homology*
  [@kaczynski2006computational].

The retinal case study uses the FIVES fundus-image dataset created by Jin and
coauthors [@jin2022fives]. These sources are cited throughout the notes where
their definitions, results, or data are used. Figures adapted from external
material are attributed individually; the remaining diagrams and experimental
plots come from my thesis.
:::
